msItem.textLang: Old Irish written in ogham script

support.desc: A silver, bossed, penannular brooch with two triangular expansions, with four lines of ogham on the reverse, dated typologically to the 9th century AD.

layoutDesc.layout: In four lines on the reverse sides of the triangular expansions of the brooch. Neatly traced on cut stem-lines — three lines on one terminal and the fourth on the other (Macalister 1945, 32). All stem-lines begin at a rivet and all but 4 (which runs past the rivet and continues after the text finishes) also end at a rivet. Lines 1 and 2 are roughly parallel (converging a little at end), running roughly horizontally L-R towards lowest rivet. The two stem-lines are the same length (aligned so start at same level), though the lower text (2) is shorter. The stem line extends all the way to the rivet but only ¾ ends up used. Line 3 rises vertically from the top of this same rivet. Line 4 (on the opposite terminal) starts at the lower rivet near the edge and runs roughly horizontally L-R towards the rim of the ring.

handDesc.handNote: As noted by Macalister (1945, 32), the X-forfid is used for all the E's except the first, and a feather-mark is prefixed to every word. Lines 1 and 2 appear to be both by the same hand, more lightly incised than 3 and 4, and more delicate letters. 3 has slightly larger and bolder lettering, 4 has distinctive, stubbier letters and a more deeply carved stem-line. The feather-mark (᚛) is used for indicating the start and direction of reading but also to indicate word/name division in 1 and 2 (but not in 4, the longest inscription, where you’d expect it). The X-forfid is used to write E in all but the first occurrence (CNAEMSXCH).

history.provenance: Found in 1806 by a peasant digging at Hill of Ballyspellan (Macalister 1945, 32).
National Museum of Ireland, where it was examined and recorded by the OG(H)AM team in February 2022.

div.p:
Cnáimsech, Cellach
Mínodor, Múad (or 'Mínodor the noble')
Máel-Maire
Máel-Ḟúataig (son of?) Máel-Maire

The object bears seven words, or ten if the three instances of MAEL are counted as separate words. These seven words could represent six or seven individual names. In contrast to the lapidary inscriptions, the names exhibit unusual pragmatical features. Their relationship to each other is unclear. Most appear to be in the nominative. Only one name in second position, MAEL-MAIRE in line 4, could conceivably be a genitive and thus qualify as a patronym. However, if Sims-Williams (1992, 51–56) is correct with his view that the forfid Ӿ was only used before non-palatalised consonants, then the analysis of this name as a masculine genitive singular is not possible, and it must rather be likewise a nominative. One word, MUAD, could be an adjective. Several of the names, but not necessarily all of them, could be those of women. Some of the names occur in royal pedigrees of the Osraige, in whose region the brooch was discovered. Perhaps the names are those of successive owners of the brooch, but the palaeography suggests that the names were engraved at perhaps two occasions. There is extensive alliteration among the words. The spelling is Old Irish.

CNAEMSECH corresponds to Old Irish cnáimsech, which is a feminine ā-stem noun meaning ‘midwife’. Even though the suffix -sech is specifically used to create feminine words for female referents or signifiés (here added to the masculine noun cnáim ‘bone’), Cnáimsech can also be used as a male name. CELLACH is the common Old Irish name Cellach, which can be used for both sexes (Ó Cuív 1986, 157). It continues Primitive Irish QENILOCI ‘having a black head, black-haired’ (see I-KER-060; Martramane, Co. Kerry). The relationship between CNAEMSECH and CELLACH, both of which are in the nominative, is unclear. Are they just mentioned one after the other, or is CELLACH the father of CNAEMSECH? In that case, his name is not in the expected genitive case. The feather-mark (᚛) between the two suggests that perhaps these should be taken as individual names but this use of the feather-mark is unconsistent and therefore unreliable.

The names MINODOR, and MUAD, if they are names at all, seem to be attested only here. MINODOR is an adjectival copulative compound (a.k.a. dvandva compound) of Old Irish min ‘small, fin, petty’ or, more likely, mín ‘smooth’ and odor ‘brown, dun’. MUAD is presumably the Old Irish adjective múad, which eDIL defines as an adjective “of uncertain meaning, confined to poetic style”, evidently with positive connotations. The meanings of both adjectives fall into semantic categories that are common among female names in Celtic (Stüber 2009, 261–265). For the use of mín in the name of a woman, cf. Mínchloth ‘of gentle reputation’ (Ó Corráin and Maguire 1990, 137; Stüber 2009, 265). If they are used as names here and are not just descriptive of one of the other names on the object, both words could therefore refer to women (again there is a, perhaps suggestive, feather-mark (᚛) between the two). A morphological argument in favour of female names is the fact that Irish appears to have the tendency to use plain adjectives for women, but derivatives in -án for men. Corresponding males names are Odrán (see I-COR-090; Underhill 3, Co. Cork) and Múadán. Perhaps MUAD is meant as an abbreviation for the male name Múadán, but this would be unusual. A female suffixal formation from the same etymon is Múadnat (Ó Corráin and Maguire 1990, 139–140).

Two different binomial names with Máel as their first element are mentioned on this object. Most names with Máel refer to men. Over 500 of them are recorded in Corpus genealogiarum Hiberniae (CGH) (O'Brien 1962, 684–695). However, this male dominance could be an illusion since our extant sources for medieval onomastics, the genealogies and the annals, are heavily skewed towards men. Two instances of Máel-Muire in Irish annals refer to women: Máel-Muire daughter of Amlaíb (Annals of Tigernach, a.d. 1021) and Máel-Muire daughter of Cináed mac Ailpín (Annals of Ulster 913.1). Ó Corráin and Maguire (1990, 130) mention two further women of that name. The runic tradition provides an interesting parallel: the name MALBRIÞA, the Old Norse adaptation of Old Irish Máel-Brigte, occurs on a brooch from Hunterston, Scotland, dating to c. 700 (Düwel and Nedoma 2023, 227), although the gender of the person cannot be determined from the contex. That same name is written MELBRIKTA on Kirk Michael II (Isle of Man; Düwel and Nedoma 2023, 229) where, however, it clearly refers to a man.

Two types of Máel names can be distinguished in Irish. The younger type, represented by MAEL-MAIRE in this inscription, has the name of a saint or another religious figure as its second element. Such names can be translated as ‘religious servant of X’ or ‘devotee of X’; the meaning derives from the primary semantics of máel ‘bald, bare’ since servants or slaves were characterised by having their hair shorn. The older type commonly has words for places or unfavourable circumstances as its second element. It is likely that the adjective máel in those cases refers to ‘new-borns, babies’, metonymically because of the bare heads that new-borns usually have. The second word seems to allude to the, often very dubious, circumstances under which a person was born or conceived. This type is illustrated by MAEL-UADAIG which probably corresponds to Old Irish Máel-Fúataig (CGH: O'Brien 1962, 690). This analysis implies that the initial f- of the second element is lenited and not written, and that D instead of Old Irish t is used to spell /d/. Old Irish fúatach is a verbal noun with the meaning ‘the act of seizing and carrying off forcibly; abducting a woman’. At some point in history, this name may have been used to refer to the offspring of a non-consensual sexual relationship. Other known bearers of this name are male.

In conclusion, for at least four names on the brooch an argument for female gender can be made (CELLACH, MINODOR, MUAD and MAEL-MAIRE), while the case for the other two (CNAEMSECH and MAEL-UADAIG) is less clear. The language of these inscriptions is Old Irish or early Middle Irish, and can belong to any time between the 8th–10th or even 11th centuries. The spelling of Máel-Ḟúataig as MAEL-UADAIG could be an innovative Middle Irish trait.
